# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains most of the engineering behind a municipal water system. A cubic meter of water weighs a metric ton, and every liter that reaches a tenth-floor apartment must be lifted against gravity, then held there under enough pressure to push it out of a faucet with satisfying force. Understanding how cities accomplish this requires a tour through elevation, energy, and the clever tricks engineers use to keep water flowing at three in the morning and at the dinner rush alike.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation as Energy

The core principle is deceptively simple: water flows from high places to low places, and pressure is just stored energy waiting to be spent. Engineers talk about "head," which is the height of a column of water, measured in meters or feet. Every 10 meters of elevation (roughly 33 feet) corresponds to about one atmosphere of pressure, or approximately 14.7 pounds per square inch. A faucet needs maybe 20 to 30 PSI to deliver a decent stream, so the water supplying a building must arrive with enough head to overcome both the height of the building and the friction losses in the pipes along the way.
